L108: To identify the dominant conceptual directions within each class, we apply Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to the projected, whitened embeddings. For each class $j\in\{\text{neg},\text{pos}\}$, we compute the following:
L109: 
L110:  | $$U_{j}\Sigma_{j}V_{j}^{\top}=\text{SVD}(X^{\prime}_{W_{j}}),$$  |
L111: where $V_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ contains the right singular vectors. We select the top-$K_{j}$ right-singular vectors $v_{1},\dots,v_{K_{j}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ from $V_{j}$ to serve as the principal directions capturing the most salient conceptual dimensions for each class. These vectors form the basis for our alignment procedure. For simplicity, we choose the same $K=K_{\text{pos}}=K_{\text{neg}}$ for both classes, tuned through validation (Tab. cite71†2 ).
L112: In this way, we obtain a balanced number of directions for both subspaces. We also evaluate the impact of varying $K$ (Tab.cite72†8 ).
L113: The alignment objective aims to find an orthogonal transformation $Q\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ such that the top-$K$ conceptual directions from each class (negative and positive) are aligned with the first $2K$ canonical axes. Let $C=[v_{1}^{(\text{neg})},\dots,v_{K}^{(\text{neg})},v_{1}^{(\text{pos})},\dots,v_{K}^{(\text{pos})}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times 2K}$ denote the set of selected concept directions, aggregated from both classes. The objective is
L114:  | $$\max_{q_{1},\dots,q_{2K}}\sum_{j=1}^{2K}q_{j}^{\top}C_{j}\mathbf{1}_{n_{j}\times 1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad Q^{\top}Q=I_{d},$$  |  | (1)
L115: where each $q_{j}$ is a column of $Q$, and $C_{j}$ is the corresponding concept direction. The goal is to align the $2K$ concept directions with the first $2K$ orthonormal axes. Thus, the orthogonal matrix $Q$ is learned such that each selected concept direction $C_{j}$ (columns of $C$) is aligned with one of the first $2K$ basis axes. In practice, this can be done by treating the $C_{j}$ as a target basis and finding the nearest orthonormal matrix (solved using another SVD or iterative optimization).
L116: This ensures that each concept is primarily represented along a single axis in the transformed space; details on how to implement this are available in (Sec. 3.3) and Algorithm 2 of [cite68†CBR20 ].
L117: Such an axis-aligned representation promotes interpretability, since each learned dimension can be associated with a distinct concept, facilitating both analysis and manipulation. each axis corresponds to a latent concept (e.g., violence, self-harm, refusal tone, etc.); we provide examples and interpretations of these concepts in Tab. cite73†5 .
L118: ### 2.1 How to remove concepts?
L119: Having aligned the feature space, we can selectively remove concepts by applying a diagonal projection matrix $P\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$. Here $P$ is a diagonal matrix with zeros for the $K$ harmful concept dimensions and ones for all other dimensions, effectively removing the harmful components.
L120: Formally, $P_{i,i}=\mathbb{I}_{i\notin\mathcal{K}}$, and $\mathbb{I}_{C}$ is the usual indicator function of statement $C$, for a set of indices $\mathcal{K}$ corresponding to the concept directions we wish to suppress. The modified representation is $\tilde{x}_{i}=PQW(x_{i}-\mu)$. Without retraining the model, we cannot pass $\tilde{x}_{i}$ directly into the subsequent layers.
L121: However, since all of these transformations except for the projection are invertible, we can recover a projected version of the embedding,
L122:  | $$\tilde{x}_{i}=W^{-1}Q^{-1}PQW(x_{i}-\mu)+\mu.$$  |
L123: 
L124: By nullifying these conceptual axes, we hypothesize a reduction in the model’s capacity to encode and process the associated behaviors, thus diminishing its ability to use them when generating text (Fig. cite70†2 ). As an ablation, we test a CALM variant without alignment (App. cite24†B ).
L125: During inference, we apply this procedure at each decoding step: we take the output embedding of the decoder for the next token, transform it via $W$ and $Q$, zero out harmful components using a projection matrix $P$, invert the transformation, and then feed the modified embedding to the softmax to produce the token distribution. This results in lightweight inference with an added complexity of $\mathcal{O}(d^{2})$ per step.
L126: The training of CALM has a total complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\max(Nd^{2},\ Td^{3}))$, where $N$ is the number of embeddings and $T$ is the number of iterations for each alignment step.
L127: ## 3 Experimental Setup
L128: #### Datasets.
L129: The LLM-LAT Harmful^{1}^{1}endnote: ^{1} cite74†https://huggingface.co/datasets/LLM-LAT/harmful-dataset†huggingface.co [cite75†SEG+24 ] dataset contains harmful prompts paired with compliant (negative) and non-compliant (positive) responses. We use 4,000 pairs to construct $X_{\text{neg}}$ and $X_{\text{pos}}$ embeddings and to evaluate perplexity before and after applying our method, referring to this dataset as Harmful Q&A.
L130: For neutral embeddings of everyday interactions, we use Alpaca [cite76†TGZ+23 ], which provides non-harmful conversation examples and yields $X_{\text{norm}}$.
L131: The declare-lab HarmfulQA^{2}^{2}endnote: ^{2} cite77†https://huggingface.co/datasets/declare-lab/HarmfulQA†huggingface.co [cite78†BP23 ] dataset covers a wide range of topics, providing both harmful and harmless conversations for each question. These dialogues explore different perspectives on each prompt. We use this dataset as a “test set” to assess model behavior in more realistic, open-ended scenarios. Throughout the paper, we refer to it as Harmful Chat.
L132: The AdvBench [cite79†ZWC+23 ] dataset is used to evaluate the practical impact of CALM. It includes 1,000 harmful prompts in two categories:
L133: 
L134: 1. Provocations:500 malicious prompts covering discrimination, profanity, graphic content, threats, misinformation, and cybercrime, testing model reactions and suggestions; 2. Harmful Behaviors:500 harmful instructions assessing compliance, advice style, disclaimers, and subtle harmful content.
L135: Neither this dataset nor Harmful Chat were used to build the concept axes; both are reserved for evaluation only.

For models prone to jailbreak behavior, we also consider an Abliterated (Abl) version. Abliteration [cite37†AOS+24 ] removes refusal behaviors by neutralizing the latent “refusal direction”, encouraging direct responses while preserving performance. Our evaluation focuses on the following: LLaMA 3 [cite80†GDJ+24 ] (8B):

L151: 
L152: We evaluate the performance of CALM across four different datasets using three distinct evaluation methods, varying the number of concepts $K$. L81: ### 2.2 System Safety Prompts
L82: 
L83: System safety prompts aim to raise model awareness of potential violations via instructions integrated into the input. For example, AdaShield cite58†Wang et al. (2024) dynamically adjusts system prompts based on request categories. The main limitation of such methods is achieving nuanced classification, and studies suggest that prompt-based defenses are often less effective than model-level alignment for complex attacks.
L84: ### 2.3 Model-Level Safety Alignment
L85: Post-training. Training-stage interventions, including supervised fine-tuning (SFT), Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) cite59†Ouyang et al. (2022) , and RLAIF, improve model safety but are limited by the availability of high-quality multimodal safety datasets. Early efforts such as VLGuard cite41†Zong et al. (2024) and SPA-VL cite42†Zhang et al. (2025a) partially address this gap, but scale and coverage remain constrained. Preference optimization techniques, including PPO cite60†Schulman et al.
L86: (2017) and DPO cite61†Rafailov et al. (2024) , have been explored for safety alignment, but multimodal preference data are still scarce.
L87: Steering. Lightweight inference-time methods compute “safety task vectors” by contrasting activations between safe and harmful inputs. cite62†Wang et al. (2025a) computes activation-level steering vectors from adversarial image triggers, VISOR cite63†Phute and Balakrishnan (2025) optimize a universal visual steering image to bias outputs toward safe behavior, and Automating Steering cite64†Wu et al. (2025) introduces an intervention matrix that dynamically corrects unsafe activations at inference.
L88: While efficient, these approaches can be task-specific and sometimes compromise model utility.
L89: ### 2.4 Output Suppression
L90: 
L91: Test-time interventions monitor generations and suppress unsafe outputs through token filtering, partial response evaluation, or best-of-$N$ selection. Methods such as ETA cite43†Ding et al. (2025) and safety re-evaluation frameworks cite44†Qi et al. (2024) enhance compliance but introduce latency and computational overhead.
L92: ### 2.5 Limitations and Motivation for SHIELD
L93: Prior work on moderation tools cite41†Zong et al. (2024) , prompt-based safeguards cite58†Wang et al. (2024) , and alignment methods cite42†Zhang et al. (2025a) either lacks explicit action guidance or incurs high computational costs. To address these limitations, we propose SHIELD, a lightweight, modular framework inspired by the principle of “deliberative safety” cite65†Guan et al. (2025) , where the reasoning model first assesses the safety of inputs based on predefined specifications before generating content.
L94: Unlike internal reasoning approaches, SHIELD implements deliberation through an explicit classifier-guided layer that assigns harmful categories and prescribes specialized rules and actions. Compared to traditional moderators, which only classify harmful inputs, SHIELD couples classification with action guidance, enabling more consistent, controllable, and nuanced responses.
L95: By integrating prompt engineering, content filters, and moderation classifiers, SHIELD provides a modular, interpretable framework that balances robustness, safety, and efficiency.
L96: ## 3 Methodology
L97: To address the limitations of prompt-only defenses and passive moderation tools, SHIELD introduces a shield-and-action pipeline that explicitly links harmful categories to enforceable responses. As illustrated in Figure cite66†4 , our framework comprises three main components: (1) safety rules, (2) safety classification with policy prioritization, and (3) safety-aware prompt composition. The classifier first assigns one or more safety categories to each input, which are then mapped to prioritized policies.
L98: SHIELD generates a composed prompt that combines the relevant safety rules with an explicit action message, which is then concatenated with the user input and passed to the LVLMs for inference. Algorithm cite67†1 summarizes the pipeline.
L99: Algorithm 1 SHIELD Pipeline
L100: 
L101: Input: User input $u=(\text{text},\text{image})$
L102: 
L103: Output: Composed prompt $P$
L104: 
L105: Classification:
L106: 
L107: $C\leftarrow$ categories detected (Violent Crimes / Malware / ...)
L108: 
L109: Policy Decision:
L110: 
L111: $d\leftarrow\texttt{hard\_block}$
L112: 
L113: $r_{p}\leftarrow\text{highest-priority rule}$
L114: 
L115: Prompt Composition:
L116: 
L117: $M_{s}\leftarrow$ safety guidance (Do / Don’t)
L118: 
L119: $M_{a}\leftarrow$ action message (block / reframe / forward)
L120: 
L121: $P\leftarrow\text{Concat}(M_{s},M_{a},u)$
L122: 
L123: return $P$
L124: ### 3.1 Safety Categories, Actions, and Instructions
L125: We adopt the harmful request taxonomy from SORRY-Bench cite68†Xie et al. (2025) , which provides comprehensive coverage of categories such as self-harm, violent crimes, and fraud. To make the taxonomy actionable, we extend it by assigning severity levels (low, medium, high) to each category. Severity levels determine whether strict refusal or guided responses are appropriate. Each category is then mapped to a system action—block, reframe, forward, or allow—according to the assessed severity.
L126: Inspired by the principle of deliberative safety cite65†Guan et al. (2025) , we enrich each harmful category with explicit Do/Don’t instructions. These instructions delineate permissible guidance from prohibited outputs, avoiding both under-refusal and excessive over-refusal. For instance, in the System Intrusion / Hacking category, the model must not provide exploit code (Don’t) but may explain general cybersecurity best practices (Do).

L88: ### 2.2 Teacher-Assisted Annotation and Relabeling
L89: 
L90: A primary contribution of our work is moving beyond the noisy, keyword-based labels prevalent in many public safety datasets. Such labels often fail to capture the context and nuance essential for accurate safety assessment, leading to high rates of false positives and negatives. To address this, we developed a teacher-assisted pipeline to systematically improve label quality at scale.
L91: Initial manual audits of the aggregated text and image datasets revealed a significant limitation in the original ground-truth labels: many annotations were based on keyword tagging rather than a holistic, contextual assessment of the content cite56†Hada et al. (2021) . Research has shown that toxicity and offensiveness are inherently context-dependent concepts that cannot be accurately assessed through simple keyword matching or surface-level pattern recognition cite57†Xenos et al.
L92: (2021a) ; cite32†Pavlopoulos et al. (2020) . The Ruddit study demonstrated that comments can vary significantly in their degree of offensiveness based on contextual factors, with the same words carrying different implications depending on their conversational and situational context cite56†Hada et al. (2021) .
L93: This often led to misclassifications where the nuance of the content was lost. Previous work has established that context can both amplify or mitigate perceived toxicity, and that a significant subset of posts (approximately 5% in controlled studies) are mislabeled when context is ignored cite32†Pavlopoulos et al. (2020) ; cite58†Xenos et al. (2021b) .
L94: To rectify this and generate rich explanatory metadata, we employed a teacher-assisted with human-in-the-loop annotation strategy using Gemini-2.5-pro cite59†Google DeepMind (2025) as the teacher model, with temperature set to 0 for deterministic outputs. For each data point, the model was prompted to generate a ‘thinking’ process and an ‘explanation’ for its classification, along with a final proposed label (Passed or Failed).
L95: This approach aligns with recent findings that context-aware evaluation significantly improves safety assessment accuracy cite57†Xenos et al. (2021a) ; cite27†Zhou et al. (2025) . Research has demonstrated that prompting models to generate intermediate reasoning steps through chain-of-thought approaches significantly improves their performance on complex reasoning tasks cite60†Wei et al.
L96: (2022) , and that training models to articulate their reasoning process enhances both accuracy and explainability cite61†OpenAI (2024) ; cite62†Bilal et al. (2024) .

L102:   * •

L115: 
L116: Our training methodology is designed to create specialized, efficient, and explainable safety classifiers. We fine-tune a multi-modal base model using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) cite64†Hu et al. (2021) to develop distinct adapters for each of our four safety categories. This section describes our model selection, the fine-tuning framework, our experimental setup with different training formats, and an analysis of the results that guided our final model selection.

L118: 
L119: We selected google/gemma-3n-E4B-it cite35†Team (2025) as our base model. Crucially, it can process not only text and images but also raw audio waveforms directly, making it an ideal candidate for our comprehensive safety system.

L157: ### 3.1 Optimising Steering with Abstention
L158: 
L159: We define steering as moving the activation $h$ in a direction that reduces the predicted error while staying close to the original $h$. Formally, we solve the following constained optimisation problem
L160: 
L161:  | $$\min_{v}\;\|v\|_{2}^{2}\quad\text{subject to}\quad\hat{p}\bigl(h+v\bigr)\,\leq\,\alpha,$$  |  | (5)
L162: 
L163: where $\alpha$ represents the target threshold of error reduction.
L164: ##### Linear Case
L165: 
L166: If $\hat{p}(h)$ is linear, i.e. $\hat{p}(h)=w^{\top}h$, this optimisation problem admits a closed-form solution as
L167: 
L168:  | $$v^{\star}\;=\;\begin{cases}0,&\text{if }w^{\top}h\;\leq\;\alpha,\\[6.0pt]
L169: \displaystyle\left(\frac{\alpha-w^{\top}h}{\|w\|_{2}^{2}}\right)\;w,&\text{if }w^{\top}h\;>\;\alpha.\end{cases}$$  |  | (6)
L170: Intuitively, if $w^{\top}h$ is already at or below $\alpha$, no intervention is required. Otherwise, we adjust $h$ to ensure $w^{\top}(h+v^{\star})$ satisfies the threshold $\alpha$.
L171: 
L172: Equivalently, we can rewrite the resulting steering vector as $v^{\star}=\lambda^{\star}w$, where
L173: 
L174:  | $$\lambda^{\star}=\max\left(0,\;\frac{\alpha-w^{\top}h}{\|w\|_{2}^{2}}\right).$$  |  | (7)
L175: 
L176: This formulation offers intuitive interpretations:
L177: 
L178:   * •
L179: Selective Steering: Intervention are applied selectively, only when $\hat{p}(h)=w^{\top}h>\alpha$ at a given token, and layer level.
L180: 
L181:   * •
L182: 
L183: Adaptive Strength: The steering strength scales with the residual $\alpha-w^{\top}h=\alpha-\hat{p}(h)$, leading to stronger adjustments for larger estimated errors.
L184: 
L185: The normalisation by $\|w\|_{2}^{2}$ aligns with prior work (cite100†von Rütte et al., 2024 ), where such scaling factors have been shown to improve steering efficacy.
L186: ##### Extension to Non-linear Models
L187: 
L188: A similar closed-form solution arises when $\hat{p}(h)$ is an affine function composed of an invertible transformation. For instance, if $\hat{p}(h)=\text{sigmoid}(w^{\top}h)$, the constraint $\hat{p}(h+v)\leq\alpha$ translates to $w^{\top}(h+v)\leq\mathrm{logit}(\alpha)$. The steering strength will be
L189: 
L190:  | $$\lambda^{\star}=\max\left(0,\;\frac{\mathrm{logit}(\alpha)-\hat{p}(h)}{\|w\|_{2}^{2}}\right)$$  |  | (8)
L191: Although we focus on linear probes in this work, §cite37†A.1 discusses how to extend these ideas to non-linear probe functions (e.g. a one-layer MLP).

L194: ### 3.2 Calibrating for Safety
L195: In this framework, the steering threshold $\alpha$ is the key parameter that determines both when an intervention is triggered, and how strongly the activations are shifted. We select $\alpha$ using a calibration set $\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{j},y_{j})\}_{j=1}^{N}$ , which is distinct from the dataset used to train the error regressor.
L196: For a given $\alpha$, let $\Delta_{\text{cal}}(\alpha)$ denote the change in some measure of LM’s performance on $\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}$, such as the accuracy $A$ (Equation cite102†2 ) or (negative) error $-E$ (Equation cite103†1 ), after applying steering with the corresponding steering strength $\lambda^{\star}$ (Equation cite104†7 ). L209: ### 3.3 A Principled Framework
L210: Our framework establishes a principled foundation for conditional activation steering, grounded in three key ingredients. First, we use linear probes to obtain effective directions for minimising the predicted error. Second, this direction is then scaled using the closed-form solution at both the token, and layer levels. Third, we calibrate the steering threshold $\alpha$ against the true error on the calibration dataset, informed by the user’s tolerance for uncertainty (i.e. set by $\delta$).
L211: A key advantage of this formulation lies in how it handles the steering strength $\lambda$: defining the appropriate range of values for this factor is nontrivial, and often requires careful weight normalisation or manual tuning. In our approach, this challenge is eliminated. The $\alpha$ value, and the estimated error inherently determine the steering strength, providing a natural, and intuitive interpretation of its role:

L217: ## 4 Choosing Representations for Steering
L218: 
L219: In the previous section, we showed how to derive a conditional steering direction for error mitigation from an arbitrary model activation $h$. A remaining question is: which representations should be used to find steering directions?
L220: The candidate set of activations $h$ is large, spanning $(n+m)\times L$, where $n+m$ denotes the total number of tokens from both the prompt, and the generated answer, and $L$ is the number of layers. Existing studies on contrastive steering navigate this extensive space by conducting computationally expensive, and model-specific hyperparameter sweeps (cite70†Li et al., 2023 ; cite89†Liu et al., 2024 ; cite74†Turner et al., 2024 ).
